piezas.titulo: Experiences of Suicide Prevention Interventions and Supports for Autistic Adults: Perspectives of Autistic Adults, Family Members and Clinicians.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Purpose Autistic adults experience disproportionately high rates of suicidality, yet little research has examined how they experience suicide prevention supports. This study explored perspectives on suicide prevention supports from Autistic adults, family members and clinicians. Methods A qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis was conducted. Semi-structured interviews were completed with 21 participants: 14 Autistic adults with lived experiences of accessing suicide prevention supports in Ireland, 4 family members and 8 clinicians working with Autistic adults experiencing suicidality. Some participants represented more than one role. Analysis was inductive, informed by a neuroaffirmative, constructivist framework and involved community engagement throughout. Results Five interconnected themes were generated. Three describe a harmful trajectory through suicide prevention supports. (1) "No one can help me", captures confusing and exclusionary help-seeking experiences. (2) "They weren't listening to me" reflects experiences of being invalidated, misunderstood, and dismissed by supports. (3) "You haven't done anything, just made it worse" describes withdrawal from future help-seeking. Across themes, systems were experienced as crisis-driven, difficult to access, and poorly attuned to Autistic distress, sometimes escalating rather than reducing distress. Two themes reflect protective buffers. (4) "Having someone who is human with you" describes how feeling understood and supported by others helped to contain suicidal distress. (5) "My whole life makes sense now" captures how developing an Autism-informed understanding of oneself reduced self-blame and fostered self-compassion. Conclusion Autism-informed, relationally attuned suicide prevention approaches that prioritise empathy, accessibility, and individualised support may reduce harm and improve engagement with suicide prevention supports for Autistic adults experiencing suicidal distress.

piezas.titulo: Agent Factory recap: Agent harnesses, shifting left, and autonomous coding
piezas.resumenOriginal: In this episode of The Agent Factory , we explore the reality of building with autonomous agents alongside Ryan Lopopolo, a software engineer at Google Cloud and the person who coined the term agent harness . From throwing out manual code editors to treating team collaboration like leveling up RPG stats, Ryan breaks down how grounding models in rich context and shifting interventions left unlocks high levels of agent autonomy. This post guides you through the key ideas from our conversation. Use it to quickly recap topics or dive deeper into specific segments with links and timestamps. The Agent Harness - What is it? Timestamp: [ 00:30 ] An AI agent as we're defining it here is a large language model (LLM) plus an agent harness . Think of the harness as everything wrapped around the LLM that isn't the model itself. For example, if you're working in Google Antigravity using Gemini 3.8 Flash , Gemini Flash is the LLM and Google Antigravity is the harness. While an unassisted model can answer simple questions out of the box, it can't check live conditions or interact with your workspace on its own. When a user asks a question like "Why is the sky blue?" , an unassisted LLM can respond without issue. However, when asked a question like "Should I wear a raincoat today?" , the model can't answer on its own because it lacks the necessary data. The harness catches the intent, queries live weather tools, bundles that context back into the prompt, and hands it to the model to produce an informed answer. Ryan Lopopolo on agent harnesses and autonomous coding Tilde Thurium sat down with Ryan Lopopolo to discuss what it takes to run fully autonomous coding workflows in production. See the summary below! Coining the harness and writing zero production code Timestamp: [ 02:22 ] The term agent harness grew out of Ryan's extensive work on autonomous coding agents, culminating in a February 2026 essay on leveraging coding models in an agent-first world. Ryan shared that he hasn't opened a traditional code editor since May of last year, maintaining that streak through his transition into Google Cloud . In this paradigm, engineers no longer author or review individual lines of syntax; instead, they operate at the level of natural language specifications and inspect the final artifacts, such as pull requests, documents, and spreadsheets. Then they determine whether the end result meets organizational standards. Harness engineering is the study and the practice of putting a model into an environment where it can succeed. If you don't do that work, you end up doing what I call 'prompt and pray'. Ryan Lopopolo Context curation and lazy prompting Timestamp: [ 03:35 ] Upfront harness investment pays off by allowing engineers to become lazy prompters. When the repository contains structured documentation, clear interfaces, and discoverable tools, you do not need to paste walls of text into a prompt box every morning "I aspire to be an incredibly lazy prompter. If I have done the job to give the model the tools and context it needs to ground itself, I don't need to write a long prompt. It figures it out." The model uses its harness to pull relevant context, allowing it to navigate large codebases and execute complex tasks without oversight. Shifting left: engineering best practices as autonomous guardrails Timestamp: [ 05:00 ] When an agent fails, developers face a whole spectrum of interventions. The most common reflex is to fiddle with the prompt or retry, but that never scales across a team. "The simplest, smooth-brain, stupidest intervention I can think of is literally just: try my prompt again without changing anything else. But shifting left means moving interventions earlier into the development lifecycle where they are cheapest and automated: from prompts, to repo docs, to linters, to tests, and all the way to upstream evals." Instead of hoping the model guesses right on the next turn, shifting left embeds standards directly into the environment. Linters, tests, and AGENTS.md files act as durable memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, making sure the agent stays on the rails without needing constant hand-holding. Leveraging established tools and determinism Timestamp: [ 06:50 ] Agents shine when they're handed tools that already mirror patterns heavily represented in pre-training data. Pairing models with standard command-line interfaces moves reasoning into determinism, shifting the burden of context aggregation away from the model and onto reliable tools. Ryan also shared an environmental design trick for context efficiency: structuring markdown files so link anchors sit directly beneath their corresponding prose blocks rather than inline. This prevents context clutter and mitigates "lost in the middle" retrieval issues. Because Ryan operates exclusively by reviewing end-state artifacts, keeping documentation readable allows him to easily inspect execution runs: "I want to be able to look at the pull request and review it. If it made a bad decision, I need to know where it went off the rails so I can whack the agent on the head and make sure it does not make that same mistake again." Long horizons and expanding the agentic loop Timestamp: [ 09:45 ] The central challenge of harness engineering is ensuring that agents cohere over long time horizons. Because human organizations produce software through iterative refinement rather than single-shot prompts, agent workflows must mirror that cadence. Harness engineering uses tightly scoped, reviewable pull requests to narrow the agent's state space. Stacking these high-confidence changes end-to-end allows supervisors to gradually expand the loop size, building trust until agents can autonomously execute large-scale initiatives, including entire language migrations Curating agent teams like RPG stats Timestamp: [ 11:58 ] Rather than divvying up sprint tasks based on individual specialties, having a diverse team contribute to an agent turns it into a central producer of work that carries everyone's strengths. Ryan compared leveling up an agent's capabilities to building out a character sheet: "[It's like] building out the stats of your RPG character. I get a new person on the team who is a React architect and boom! The attention that they pay is able to bump out the stats in front-end architecture and performance." With that collective expertise baked into the environment, the agent can autonomously classify incoming work and activate the exact skills it needs on demand, operating as both a backend architect and a front-end specialist. Accruing leverage in tools, not custom harnesses Timestamp: [ 14:38 ] For developers wondering whether to build their own custom agent harness, Ryan offered clear advice: don't build one from scratch. Standard harnesses already provide the foundational primitives: file reading, grep search, and command execution. Over-scaffolding an agent with rigid, bespoke frameworks creates technical debt and leads to sunk-cost traps when frontier models advance. "If you focus all of your efforts on improving quality on tools and context, you can freely adopt the newest models as they come out and you'll be constantly accruing leverage into a bit of the system that will never become obsolete." Operating Google Cloud and eliminating capability overhang Timestamp: [ 16:47 ] Discussing his work at Google Cloud , Ryan outlined his motivation to eliminate capability overhang : the delta between what frontier AI models are theoretically capable of and how much useful work is currently extracted in production. Because the cloud functions as a massive, programmable surface, equipping agents with direct interfaces to Google Cloud lets them manage and deploy infrastructure effectively, turning raw model capability into tangible enterprise utility. Continually updating your priors on AI Timestamp: [ 18:13 ] The speed of AI development requires engineers and teams to actively unlearn old limitations and constantly reassess what these models can achieve. " It's very important to continually be updating what you think is possible with these lovely tools that we have ," Ryan urged. What broke six months ago often runs effortlessly on today's frontier models. Rather than getting locked into rigid workflows, developers should build around the two highly extensible interfaces that will remain relevant across every model upgrade: tools and context. "Agents will always need context in order to do that last mile adaptation into what you think good is. And as you can continue to... shift it to the left, in terms of increasingly capable tools which act as a form of memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, you'll continually be amazed as the models are able to do more and more interesting things for you over time." How To Build A Custom Harness Next, Billy Jacobson started us off by showing how developers can customize their own agent harnesses for specific tasks. Under the hood: Why build a custom harness? Timestamp: [ 19:44 ] Before jumping into code, Billy unpacked why developers should understand the mechanics of a harness rather than treating it like a black box. Recalling advice from an engineering mentor that "You can just use the framework, but a great engineer will really understand the framework" , Billy explained that building a harness yourself is the best way to debug what happens when an agent breaks. You can evaluate three core design decisions for every workflow: Looping : How many iterations should the agent run, and what conditions trigger an exit state? Tools : What specific tools should the agent access, and when and how should it invoke them? Memory : How important is conversational and operational memory, and when should it be retrieved or compacted? Linear Agent Harness: Deterministic Single-Pass Execution Timestamp: [ 21:34 ] Billy demonstrated a minimalist linear harness designed for deterministic workflows where looping is unnecessary. This pattern is ideal for targeted inspections, file transformations, or single-turn data analyses where you want a high level of determinism and need the agent to perform the exact same execution flow every single time. Closed-Loop Agent Harness: Iterative Test-Driven Repair Timestamp: [ 22:45 ] When tasks demand active bug fixing and refactoring, a closed-loop harness provides the iterative reasoning required to reach a verified resolution. In this demo, Billy showcased an agent that applies an automated code edit to address a failing requirement, and the harness executes the unit test suite against the updated codebase. If the tests fail, the runtime captures standard failure logs and detailed stack traces, feeding those error diagnostics directly back into the agent's working memory. The process repeats continuously until all unit tests pass, backed by a five-iteration ceiling to prevent infinite loops and runaway execution costs. Guardrail Harness with Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) Timestamp: [ 23:25 ] For developers who require custom behavior without rewriting core orchestration plumbing from scratch, Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) provides scaffolding with automated memory management and execution safeguards. Billy walked through an example that leverages ADK's native context compaction to summarize older conversational turns, preventing context window bloat during extended debugging runs. Custom interception hooks inspect and filter shell actions before execution, automatically stopping high-risk operations such as recursive file deletions, database drops, or unauthorized remote git pushes. This architecture gives teams fine-grained control over tool execution boundaries while avoiding the maintenance burden of bespoke harness frameworks. The 3-Layer Agent Dev Stack: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google Antigravity, and Google Skills Timestamp: [ 25:27 ] Next up, Smitha Kolan broke down why coding agents do not always require heavier reasoning models, emphasizing that high performance stems from balancing the three layers of the agent stack: Model , Harness , and Knowledge . "Your coding agent doesn't need a smarter model. It needs a better stack: model, harness, and knowledge. When all three click into place, everything changes." She then walked through the three tools she's been loving recently, one for each layer of the stack. Layer 1 | Model | Gemini 3.8 Flash : High-frequency agentic loops run between 20 and 60 sequential hops per task (inspecting files, updating functions, and executing unit tests). Because latency and API costs compound across iterations, a lightweight, responsive model like Gemini 3.8 Flash makes real-time agent loops practical without running up a massive bill. Layer 2 | Harness | Google Antigravity with /boost : Default Antigravity handles standard navigation and component creation. On top of that, the /boost command spins up an orchestrator that coordinates specialized sub-agents in parallel and concludes with an independent audit pass before modifying files. Layer 3 | Knowledge | Google Skills Repository : With over 19,000 GitHub stars and 100+ curated domain packages across Google Cloud, Firebase, Flutter, and Maps, this harness-agnostic repository injects precise domain context on demand, preventing agents from guessing cloud configurations Your turn to build Building effective coding agents requires moving past the reflex of simply swapping in larger models. As Ryan Lopopolo's philosophy of harness engineering illustrates, true developer leverage is achieved by shifting best practices to the left and investing in rich tools, deterministic verifiers, and well-curated context that survive model upgrades. When combined with fast inference models, structured orchestration harnesses, and modular domain knowledge, agents evolve from conversational novelties into dependable, autonomous engineering partners. Ready to put it into practice? Explore the tools and resources covered in this episode: Gemini 3.8 Flash : Fast, low-cost model for multi-hop agent loops. Google Antigravity ( /boost ): Orchestrator harness for parallel coding agents and verification. Google Skills : Modular domain knowledge for Google Cloud, Firebase, and Flutter. piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Voluntary physical activity and pharmacological treatment with the Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 alleviate regional alterations in cerebral synaptic density and improve behavioral recovery after unilateral labyrinthectomy in the rat
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundUnilateral peripheral vestibular loss induces adaptive mechanisms of cerebral plasticity. The quantified Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761® has been shown to enhance neural plasticity, and is used in the treatment of vertigo and dizziness. We here aimed to investigate, how voluntary physical training in a running wheel (RWT) and oral treatment with EGb 761® affect behavioral recovery and whole-brain synaptic density following chemical unilateral labyrinthectomy (cUL) in the rat.MethodsThirty-two Sprague Dawley rats were divided into 4 groups with different treatment regimens (group 1: control food; group 2: control food + RWT; group 3: EGb 761® food (75mg/day/kg body weight); group 4: EGb 761® food + RWT). All rats underwent a left-sided cUL by transtympanic injection of bupivacaine and p-arsanilic acid. Behavioral testing (scoring of nystagmus, postural asymmetry, head tilt, locomotion tracking in open field) was done weekly until 9 weeks (d63) after cUL. Serial [18F]UCB-H μPET imaging of synaptic density (targeting synaptic vesicular protein 2A) was performed before and up to 9 weeks post cUL. Images were whole-brain normalized and segmented based on Schiffer's atlas. Voxel-wise and regional changes of cerebral [18F]UCB-H uptake were compared across groups and time points.ResultsAll rats showed signs of acute vestibular syndrome following cUL. The EGb 761® + RWT group had a significantly faster and more complete improvement of postural asymmetry by week 5 post UL and a higher locomotor velocity thereafter than the control food group. Compared to baseline, at d63 post cUL the EGb 761® group showed the smalles reduction of synaptic density in the vestibular nuclei of−7.59 ± 7.0 % (vs.−20.37 ± 5.18% in control food group, p < 0.001). In contrast, at d63 post cUL the motor cortex displayed the highest relative gain of synaptic density in the control food group (6.6 ± 3.13 % vs. 0.19 ± 2.81% in the EGb 761® group, p < 0.001). All treatment groups showed an increase of synaptic density in the hippocampal area and the somatosensory cortex at weeks 1-3 post cUL compared to the control food group. The additive effect of EGb 761® and RWT was statistically confirmed in behavior and PET measurements.ConclusionsUnilateral labyrinthectomy induces loss of synaptic density in vestibulo-cerebellar networks, which can be partially reversed by EGb 761® treatment. Combined physical and EGb 761® treatment improves behavioral recovery from cUL most effectively, reinforcing the importance of multimodal treatment in acute vestibulopathies.

piezas.titulo: How Top-Down Are We? Reconsidering the Gap Between Occupational Therapy's Identity and Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Occupational therapy has spent more than a century defining occupation as its professional core. Yet studies across countries and settings show a recurring gap. Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. This article argues that the profession may face a translation problem more than an identity problem. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Bottom-up methods are not inherently incompatible with occupational therapy; the problem arises when change in a component is treated as sufficient evidence of occupational success. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.

piezas.titulo: ScyllaDB in Enterprise Java: High-Performance NoSQL With Eclipse JNoSQL
piezas.resumenOriginal: Modern enterprise applications must process increasing data volumes while guaranteeing low latency, high availability, and predictable performance. While relational databases are essential for transactional workloads and complex queries, some applications do not fit the relational model. Systems that manage millions of user engagements, financial events, or IoT data often need a persistence solution built for distributed environments and horizontal scalability. In these cases, ScyllaDB affords a compelling option for enterprise architects. ScyllaDB is a high-performance, distributed NoSQL database based on the wide-column data model. Inspired by Apache Cassandra and compatible with its query language (CQL), ScyllaDB uses a shard-per-core architecture to maximize hardware efficiency and preserve consistent performance under intensive workloads. When should ScyllaDB be chosen over traditional relational databases or other NoSQL options? This article examines its column-family model, compares it with Cassandra, and shows how to integrate ScyllaDB into a Java enterprise application.

piezas.titulo: Master AI Chip Principles With New IEEE Design Program
piezas.resumenOriginal: Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “ Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges .” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments. The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations. To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks. One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance. The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall —has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms. No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency. The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program , developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society . Topics covered The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment. The topics are: Fundamental principles of design and functionality. Practical insights into advanced architectures. Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment. Emerging trends and evolving architectures. Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT). The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems. It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments. The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments. By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. AI-generated avatars explain concepts The program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action. A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect. In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments. By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. Research published in 2024 in IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies showed that avatar‑based instruction can increase a learner’s confidence by up to 25 percent and improve retention of complex technical material. Each course concludes with a module in which the two experts from different disciplines debate, question, and challenge each other’s assumptions. Modeling expert reasoning through dialogue The cross‑disciplinary conversations can do more than explain concepts; they can model how experts think. They can reveal the negotiations behind architectural choices, the competing priorities that shape system design, and the analytical rigor required to balance performance, efficiency, scalability, and compliance. Learners observe engineering discourse, gaining insight into the reasoning patterns that drive innovation in AI processor development. The program goes further by interrupting the dialogue at key moments and inviting the learner to step in. Instead of passively absorbing information, the learner decides how to resolve a trade‑off, predict the outcome of a design choice, or select the most defensible engineering path. The experience can feel less like a course and more like an apprenticeship inside an engineering team. A new standard for advanced engineering education By merging rigorous technical content with an innovative, dialogue‑driven delivery model, the program sets a standard for teaching advanced engineering. It captures the complexity of real‑world problem‑solving, humanizes the learning experience, and challenges participants to think like the engineers who are defining the future of AI hardware. It is not simply a new course; it is a new way of learning. For individual access, visit the IEEE Learning Network . piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

piezas.titulo: Targeting the RNA regulator HuR in acute traumatic brain injury mitigates secondary injury and improves functional outcome by suppressing neuroinflammation
piezas.resumenOriginal: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) affects ~2.5 million people annually in the US. Minutes after TBI, microglia and astrocytes initiate a neuroinflammatory cascade which promotes secondary injury via cytotoxicity, blood-brain barrier damage, edema, and immune cell recruitment. HuR, an RNA regulator, plays a critical role in the glial response by promoting the expression of proinflammatory mediators including IL-6, IL-1{beta}, TNF-, COX-2, CCL2, and CXCL1 via adenine and uridine-rich elements in the 3' untranslated region of their mRNAs. Here, we assessed SRI-42127, a small molecule HuR inhibitor developed by our group, on neuroinflammatory responses, secondary injury, and functional outcome after TBI. Male mice underwent controlled cortical impact (CCI) followed by peripheral administration of SRI-42127. Functional outcomes assessed included: motor function (balance beam/rotarod) and memory function (object location/recognition). Edema, lesion volume, and BBB permeability were assessed by MRI, brain water content, and Evans blue dye extravasation. HuR nucleocytoplasmic translocation, neuronal loss/apoptosis, microglial and astrocyte activation, and neutrophil infiltration were quantified by immunohistochemistry. Proinflammatory mediator induction was assessed by RT-qPCR and/or immunoblot. Results showed that SRI-42127 treatment improved spatial memory and fine motor performance in the first week in parallel with a reduction in edema, vascular permeability, lesion size, and neuronal loss/apoptosis. There was attenuated microglial activation and astrogliosis, decreased neutrophil infiltration, and suppression of proinflammatory mediator induction. Mechanistically, SRI-42127 inhibited HuR nucleocytoplasmic translocation in microglia and astrocytes. In summary, SRI-42127 potently suppresses neuroinflammation and secondary injury after TBI, improves functional outcomes, and identifies HuR as a new therapeutic target in TBI.

piezas.titulo: Sensory Processing Differences in Children With Idiopathic Toe Walking: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceThe cause of idiopathic toe walking (ITW) remains unclear, though impaired sensory processing has often been hypothesized to be linked to ITW.ObjectivesThe objective of this article is to review the literature on toe-walking to identify how sensory processing contributes to ITW.Data SourcesFour databases (CINAHL, Pubmed, PsychINFO, and SCOPUS) were searched for papers related to sensory processing and ITW published prior to July 2024. References of retrieved papers were reviewed for additional sources.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe PRISMA guidelines for scoping review were used to abstract the data following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Inclusion criteria were examined and papers included at least one sensory system related to ITW was studied. Papers were excluded if toe walking was due to diagnosed neurological, orthopedic, or genetic conditions.FindingsOur scoping review identified 13 published articles relevant to examining sensory processing in children with ITW. Studies explored differences in vibration perception, light touch, proprioception, vestibular, visual processing, sensorimotor functional assessments, and parental surveys of sensory processing. Six of the papers were included in a meta-analysis on vibration perception threshold that failed to reach significance ( p = .12). Despite heterogeneity across studies in participants, methods, and outcomes, a meta-analysis for atypical scores from parent-report sensory processing survey data yielded significant differences between children with ITW and typical controls ( p < .0068).Conclusions and RelevanceChildren with ITW demonstrate impairments across multiple domains of sensory processing and sensory-motor function suggesting an underlying relationship between ITW and sensory differences. Children with ITW, however, represent a diverse group of individuals with significant between-subjects variability in which senses are impaired, and which outcome measures best capture these differences.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Boletín de vulnerabilidades Vulnerabilidades con productos recientemente documentados: No hay vulnerabilidades nuevas para los productos a los que está suscrito. Otras vulnerabilidades de los productos a los que usted está suscrito, y cuya información ha sido actualizada recientemente: Vulnerabilidad en productos Mozilla (CVE-2017-5436) Severidad: ALTA Fecha de publicación: 11/06/2018 Fecha de última actualización: 16/10/2026 Se desencadena una escritura fuera de límites en la biblioteca Graphite 2 con una fuente Graphite maliciosamente manipulada. Esto resulta en un cierre inesperado potencialmente explotable. Este problema se solucionó en la biblioteca Graphite 2, así como en los productos Mozilla. La vulnerabilidad afecta a Thunderbird en versiones anteriores a la 52.1, Firefox ESR en versiones anteriores a la 45.9, Firefox en versiones anteriores a la 52.1 y Firefox en versiones anteriores a la 53. Vulnerabilidad en kernel de Linux (CVE-2023-50431) Severidad: MEDIA Fecha de publicación: 09/12/2023 Fecha de última actualización: 16/10/2026 sec_attest_info en drivers/accel/habanalabs/common/habanalabs_ioctl.c en el kernel de Linux hasta 6.6.5 permite una fuga de información al espacio del usuario porque info->pad0 no está inicializado. Vulnerabilidad en kernel de Linux (CVE-2024-0607) Severidad: MEDIA Fecha de publicación: 18/01/2024 Fecha de última actualización: 16/10/2026 Se encontró una falla en el subsistema Netfilter en el kernel de Linux. El problema está en la función nft_byteorder_eval(), donde el código itera a través de un bucle y escribe en la matriz `dst`. En cada iteración, se escriben 8 bytes, pero `dst` es una matriz de u32, por lo que cada elemento solo tiene espacio para 4 bytes. Eso significa que cada iteración sobrescribe parte del elemento anterior, lo que posiblemente lleve a una escritura fuera de los límites. Esta falla permite que un usuario local provoque una denegación de servicio o potencialmente aumente sus privilegios en el sistema. Vulnerabilidad en m2crypto (CVE-2023-50781) Severidad: ALTA Fecha de publicación: 05/02/2024 Fecha de última actualización: 15/10/2026 Se encontró una falla en m2crypto. Este problema puede permitir que un atacante remoto descifre mensajes capturados en servidores TLS que utilizan intercambios de claves RSA, lo que puede provocar la exposición de datos confidenciales o sensibles. Vulnerabilidad en kernel de Linux (CVE-2024-35809) Severidad: MEDIA Fecha de publicación: 17/05/2024 Fecha de última actualización: 15/10/2026 En el kernel de Linux, se ha resuelto la siguiente vulnerabilidad: PCI/PM: drena las devoluciones de llamada inactivas en tiempo de ejecución antes de eliminar el controlador. Una condición de ejecución entre la devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() y la devolución de llamada .remove() en el controlador PCI rtsx_pcr conduce a un crash de kernel debido a un error de página no controlado [1]. El problema es que no se espera que rtsx_pci_runtime_idle() se ejecute después de llamar a pm_runtime_get_sync(), pero esto último realmente no garantiza eso. Solo garantiza que las devoluciones de llamada de suspensión y reanudación no se ejecutarán cuando regrese. Sin embargo, si ya se está ejecutando una devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() cuando se llama a pm_runtime_get_sync(), este último notará que el estado de PM en tiempo de ejecución del dispositivo es RPM_ACTIVE y regresará de inmediato sin esperar a que se complete el primero. De hecho, no puede esperar a que se complete .runtime_idle() porque puede ser llamado desde esa devolución de llamada (podría decirse que no tiene mucho sentido hacerlo, pero no está estrictamente prohibido). Por lo tanto, en general, quien proporciona una devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() debe protegerla para que no se ejecute en paralelo con cualquier código que se ejecute después de pm_runtime_get_sync(). [Tenga en cuenta que .runtime_idle() no se iniciará después de que pm_runtime_get_sync() haya regresado, pero puede continuar ejecutándose si comenzó antes.] Una forma de abordar esa condición de ejecución es llamar a pm_runtime_barrier() después de pm_runtime_get_sync() (no antes porque es necesario un valor distinto de cero del contador de uso de PM en tiempo de ejecución para evitar que se invoquen devoluciones de llamada de PM en tiempo de ejecución) para esperar a que se complete la devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() en caso de que se esté ejecutando en ese punto. Un lugar adecuado para hacerlo es pci_device_remove() que llama a pm_runtime_get_sync() antes de eliminar el controlador, por lo que también puede llamar a pm_runtime_barrier() posteriormente, lo que evitará que se produzca la ejecución en cuestión, no sólo en el controlador rtsx_pcr, sino en cualquier controlador PCI que proporcione devoluciones de llamada .runtime_idle(). piezas.titulo: Are clinician-administered ataxia scales truly culture-free? Rethinking contextual validity in diverse populations
piezas.resumenOriginal: Hereditary cerebellar ataxias are genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous progressive neurodegenerative disorders characterized by substantial functional impairment. With the emergence of disease-modifying therapies and gene-targeted clinical trials, standardized and reliable clinical outcome measures are essential for assessing disease severity and progression. Among the available scales, two are widely used by clinicians to assess ataxia: The Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) and the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS). Given considerable linguistic, educational and sociocultural heterogeneity across the globe, we opine that it may pose challenges to the uniform application and cross-cultural comparability of these instruments. Published translations and adaptations were also examined to determine whether cultural adaptation extended beyond linguistic translation. Among all the identified adaptations, reported processes predominantly comprised forward and backward translation, expert review and assessment of linguistic, conceptual or cultural equivalence. These findings suggest that linguistic translation alone may not be sufficient to ensure that clinician-rated ataxia scales retain equivalent meaning and measurement across diverse populations. We therefore introduce the concept of “contextual validity” emphasizing that language, educational heterogeneity, literacy, graphomotor familiarity, cultural practices and testing environments that may influence performance independently of cerebellar dysfunction. This perspective outlines considerations for developing contextually adapted and psychometrically validated Indian-language versions of SARA and ICARS to improve measurement accuracy and support equitable clinical assessment and participation in global clinical trials.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede una escala de ataxia medir igual en todas las culturas? piezas.titulo: Transient cortical activity modulates somatosensory gating during postural control
piezas.resumenOriginal: Human somatosensory responses vary with movement-related gating as well as with fluctuations in ongoing cortical activity. During standing, both somatosensory responses and cortical activity change in response to postural demands. However, little is known regarding whether moment-to-moment fluctuations in cortical activity contribute to variation in somatosensory responses during different postural tasks. In this study, we investigated whether somatosensory-evoked potentials (SEPs) during postural control are associated with prestimulus cortical activity, focusing on oscillatory amplitudes and corticocortical connectivity. SEPs evoked by tibial nerve stimulation were recorded in 18 healthy adults under four postural conditions. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) was used to extract single-trial SEP amplitudes from multichannel electroencephalography (EEG). The results showed that the early component of CCA-SEPs, N80, was significantly reduced according to postural demands. A higher prestimulus amplitude in the {beta}-frequency band in the central cortical regions was associated with a larger N80 amplitude. Moreover, modulation of -band corticocortical connectivity involving frontal and parietal regions covaried with N80 reduction. Clustering analysis using {beta}-amplitude and -connectivity as features further indicated that multivariate prestimulus cortical activity accounted for variability in N80 amplitude. These findings revealed that somatosensory responses vary through posture-related somatosensory gating and as a function of ongoing fluctuations in cortical activity. Clarifying the temporal dynamics of somatosensory processing will help elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of standing balance and contribute to the development of novel physiological assessments of postural impairments.

piezas.titulo: Prefrontal cortical morphometric covariance and cognitive task performance in healthy young adults: an exploratory analysis of Human Connectome Project data
piezas.resumenOriginal: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). Oblimin-rotated principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to residualized thickness and surface area for 22 PFC regions, controlling for age, sex, and ICV. Component scores were entered as predictors in separate regression models for the Flanker Age-Adjusted Score (inhibitory control), the Gambling RT Difference (RT for the same “larger” guess in reward minus punishment blocks), and 2-Back median RT (working memory speed). Parallel analysis favored two thickness components; a prespecified three-component solution (Global/Lateral PFC, RC1; Orbitofrontal, RC2; Anterior Cingulate, RC3; 53.7% of variance) was retained by decision, and RC1 and RC2 were only moderately stable across bootstrap resamples. RC1 was nominally associated with lower Flanker scores (β = −0.103, p = 0.027), opposite to the predicted direction, and RC2 with a smaller Gambling RT Difference (β = −0.103, p = 0.025); neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q = 0.054). In uncorrected models added at review, whole-cortex mean thickness alone robustly predicted Flanker scores but not the Gambling RT Difference; neither component association survived regressing mean thickness out before PCA. In surface area analyses, greater orbitofrontal surface area (AC2) was associated with faster 2-Back RT (β = −0.125, p = 0.003; q = 0.032 across 12 surface area tests and 0.064 across all 24 component tests), not explained by a speed-accuracy tradeoff. This unpredicted association persisted in most sensitivity analyses but was attenuated and non-significant when total surface area was regressed out before PCA (β = −0.065, p = 0.078). In conclusion, no prefrontal-specific association was robust. Global cortical thickness accounts for the Flanker association more parsimoniously, the Gambling RT Difference association was not robust under either account, and the orbitofrontal surface area association could not be separated from global surface area; all associations require replication.

destilado.texto: Descubrir que la superficie orbitofrontal se asocia a respuestas más rápidas en la prueba de dos dígitos cambia la visión de la corteza prefrontal. El estudio, con datos del proyecto Human Connectome y publicado en Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, sugiere una vía para mejorar la rapidez cognitiva sin perder precisión.

piezas.titulo: "It cannot depend solely on the parents"-professionals' perspectives on patient journeys of children with chronic conditions across health and social care in Germany.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Purpose Professionals in healthcare, social services and the education system are confronted with a growing number of children with chronic conditions. Complex treatment plans, care coordination and cross-system care needs result in additional demands on professionals. This study aimed to explore professionals' perspectives on the patient journeys of children with chronic conditions in Germany and identify opportunities to improve care. Methods This qualitative study used semi-structured interviews conducted from May 2023 to February 2024. A purposive sample of professionals working with children with chronic conditions (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, developmental disorders, cerebral palsy, bronchial asthma, type 1 diabetes) was recruited from the health, social care, and education systems in Germany. Sampling was guided by an assessment of thematic saturation. Data were analysed using structuring qualitative content analysis. Results Twenty-two professionals participated, including physicians (n = 7), therapists (n = 8) and social workers and counsellors (n = 7). Care was perceived as fragmented, difficult to navigate, and poorly coordinated across health, social care, and education systems. Key barriers included long waiting times, unclear care pathways, and limited interprofessional communication. Greater difficulties in navigating care and support were perceived among families facing socioeconomic disadvantage or language barriers. Conclusion Professionals perceived current care structures as insufficiently meeting the needs of children with chronic conditions, particularly where families face greater barriers to navigating services. Strengthening cross-system coordination and accessibility may improve patient journeys. Future research should examine how barriers vary according to socioeconomic circumstances and across stages of the patient journey and evaluate condition-independent approaches to improving care. Trial registration This study was registered in the German Clinical Trials Register, ID: DRKS00032139, on 07 November 2023. What is known • Research on patient journeys of children with chronic conditions has primarily focused on individual, often rare, conditions. • Evidence spanning multiple chronic conditions and the healthcare, social services, and education systems remains highly limited. What is new • Drawing on diverse professionals' perspectives, this study provides a cross-system, cross-condition view of paediatric patient journeys. • It identifies common barriers to care coordination and access across systems and diagnoses, highlighting actionable opportunities for integrated care.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades): T.A.C.T is a 501(c)(3) that provides trade and technical skills to children, young adults and families living with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. piezas.titulo: Fragments: September 16
piezas.resumenOriginal: Reports of agentic hacking continue, in this case it happened back in May and it seems OpenAI did not disclose that they were responsible. Simon Willison sees two options: After the Hugging Face and Wiki attacks OpenAI were still unable to review their previous logs and determine that they had previously attacked RubyGems. They knew about the attack on RubyGems and made the decision not to reach out to the RubyGems team about it. Both of these are bad! Given this incident, the Hugging Face situation, and the Wiki attack, the obvious question right now is how many more incidents like this are out there waiting to be discovered? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Dave Farley: Stop asking the sci-fi question: ‘Is it conscious?’ Start asking the engineering question: ‘Is this a powerful, unpredictable component being put somewhere consequential, and where’s the feedback that tells us that it’s safe? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Nate Silver is known for his forecasts, but to do them he writes a lot of code for his models. He’s found agentic engineering capable of doing miraculous work . In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter. The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence. Consider the Hugging Face attack. Although these agents showed remarkable intelligence, they weren’t really super-intelligent - but they were super-persistent. This is a common theme of AI in its various forms: Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities As we try to figure out what kind of regulations we need to keep AI under control, we need to remember that we should design our guards around super-persistence as much as worrying about super-intelligence. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ “Uncle Bob” Martin has made many posts on X during the last few months about his programming with LLMs. His approach has been to build a firm harness to keep them under control, so they create software that is maintainable as well as functional. Sadly the posts have been frustratingly light on detail. But now it seems that lack of information may not matter And while I was heads-down getting that to work, the agents got a LOT better. So much so that when I came up for air, the need for my harness was obviated. Indeed, the need for any but the most liberal of harnesses may be obviated. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Some tidbits that struck me from Ezra Klein’s recent (recommended) interview with Matt Sheehan on the interplay between regulation of AI and competition with China . While Chinese models have made some surprisingly remarkable gains in the slipstream of US frontier models, the US still has 8 times as much compute available to it than China - which is a material gap. People in the US worry that regulation will slow down the US model builders, but these rapid recent gains in China have occurred under much more regulation Americans say that when they set up a hotline to talk to Chinese leaders in a crisis, the Chinese don’t pick up the phone. But this misunderstands the Chinese system. Individual Chinese, even powerful ones, aren’t given individual decision-making power. They operate with committees and documents. So the Americans are better off sending a fax than trying to call an individual Like so many things, effective regulation needs regular practice When American policymakers are like: Where do you start? — I sometimes say: Well, you start by starting. You learn how to regulate things, you learn how to legislate on them by regulating and legislating on them.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de inteligencia: la persistencia de los agentes también cambia el panorama. Fowler señala que OpenAI ocultó un ataque a RubyGems pese a conocerlo. La falta de retroalimentación de seguridad dificulta detectar incidentes futuros.

piezas.titulo: Preoperative cranial computed tomography in pediatric cochlear implantation: clinical necessity or optional step?
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectivesDue to growing evidence regarding the risks of ionizing radiation, especially in children, some centers now perform cochlear implantation (CI) without a preoperative computed tomography (CT) scan, relying solely on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study evaluates the necessity and safety of omitting CT scans before bilateral CI in children.MethodsA retrospective analysis of 164 children, implanted bilaterally between 2018 and 2024 and aged under 10 years at the time of either simultaneous or second CI, were included. The impact of preoperative imaging on duration of surgery and perioperative complications was analyzed. The surgical procedure was compared between cases with and without a preoperative CT scan and analyzed for surgeons in training and experienced surgeons.Results105 children were implanted with a preoperative CT scan and 59 without a CT scan. The duration of bilateral CI surgery was 122.5 (±41.4) min for procedures [CI without CT: 122.5 (±41.4) min; CI with CT: 116.1 (±33.84) min; (p = 0.4861)] and anesthesia [CI without CT: 237.2 (±47.38) min; CI with CT: 226.3 (±41.50) min; (p = 0.1352)] did not differ significantly between the groups, irrespective of the experience of the surgeons. Seven cases showed relevant malformations visible on MRI, such as large vestibular aqueduct syndrome, which were relevant during the surgery. Minor and major complications occurred rarely in both cohorts but more frequently in patients without CT scan (without CT: 10.2% (6/59); with CT: 4.8% (5/105); p = 0.2052; risk difference [RD], 5.4%; 95% CI, −6.3 to 14.3%). Intraoperative X-ray imaging revealed no cases of electrode tip fold-over, and no patients developed postoperative complete or incomplete facial nerve palsy.ConclusionIn summary, an MRI-based imaging strategy without routine preoperative CT may be safe and sufficient in appropriately selected pediatric CI candidates, with additional CT reserved for patients in whom clinical or MRI findings suggest relevant bony abnormalities, complex inner ear malformations, or syndromic conditions. This approach reduces unnecessary radiation exposure and the use of healthcare resources, while avoiding redundant diagnostic information from both imaging modalities, without compromising surgical safety or outcomes.

piezas.titulo: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
piezas.resumenOriginal: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

piezas.titulo: Astrocytic ablation of truncated TrkB receptors reduces amyloid plaques and prevents synaptic loss in 5xFAD mice
piezas.resumenOriginal: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is essential for nervous system development and function and exerts its effects primarily through the tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB). The Ntrk2 gene encodes a full-length receptor (TrkB.FL) and two truncated isoforms (TrkB.T1 and TrkB.T2, collectively TrkB.T) that lack the intracellular tyrosine kinase domain. TrkB.T is expressed predominantly in astrocytes and is thought to inhibit BDNF-TrkB.FL signaling by sequestering BDNF and forming signaling-deficient heterodimers with TrkB.FL. Here, we investigated whether selective ablation of astrocytic TrkB.T could ameliorate Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology by enhancing endogenous BDNF-TrkB.FL signaling. Astrocyte-specific deletion of the Ntrk2 gene at 5 weeks of age reduced cortical TrkB.T expression by more than 80% without affecting TrkB.FL levels. TrkB.T ablation increased the size of Bassoon-positive presynaptic active zones, consistent with enhanced BDNF-TrkB.FL signaling. Remarkably, astrocytic TrkB.T ablation reduced {beta}-amyloid plaque burden by more than 60% in the cortex, hippocampus, and subiculum of 6-month-old 5xFAD mice, despite having no detectable effect on microgliosis or astrogliosis. Furthermore, TrkB.T ablation prevented reductions in the density and size of PSD-95-positive postsynaptic sites in the cortex and hippocampus of 5xFAD mice at 1 year old. Together, these findings identify astrocytic TrkB.T as an important regulator of amyloid pathology and synaptic integrity in an AD mouse model. Our results suggest that selectively reducing TrkB.T expression represents a promising therapeutic strategy to enhance endogenous neuroprotective BDNF-TrkB.FL signaling, reduce amyloid pathology, and preserve synaptic integrity in AD.
