piezas.titulo: From a surgeon's stroke to a third hemisphere—The auxilium architecture for brain restoration and extension
piezas.resumenOriginal: A surgeon was exercising on a stationary bicycle when he had a large ischemic left middle cerebral artery territory stroke, complicated by hemorrhagic transformation requiring hemicraniectomy and cranioplasty. He developed right-sided spastic hemiplegia and a mixed aphasia. This paper takes that case as its anchor to pose the question: beyond improving residual function, what would it mean to restore cognitive function that was lost so that the person fully returns to their pre-stroke baseline? Existing brain-computer interfaces rely on the person having an intact cortical substrate for intended movement and speech. Here we propose the Auxilium, a brain restoration architecture for the situation where that substrate is no longer present: an extracranial auxiliary brain system, agnostic to its substrate, that connects to a person's residual cortex through whatever input-output technology proves most appropriate, and that supplies, in parallel and in real time, new substrate, whether biological or synthetic. We address an assumption of brain-computer interface development, that throughput is the binding constraint. Linking a kHz brain to MHz digital does not impart the higher clock speed, because the limitation lies not in the port but in the architecture of the entire brain and body imparted by evolution. We posit that the substrate of canonical circuits and their integration areas is essential, and the Auxilium can be understood as restoring both connectivity (linkage between disconnected areas) and computation (information generation capability of a volume of neural tissue). We propose a near-term de-risking pipeline using stereoelectroencephalography during surgical epilepsy evaluation, comparing extracranial modules spanning threshold rules, PID controllers, expert systems, artificial neural networks, neuromorphic devices, and biological specimens, each linked in real time to a participant serving as their own control on naturalistic tasks. If ports alone restore the lost function, the requirement is routing connectivity. If performance improves only when the module supplies its own dynamics, the requirement is computational substrate. We expect the answer to depend on how much tissue was lost, how quickly, and on the individual's reserve, and we treat routing and substrate as endpoints of a continuum to be mapped empirically.

Autistic individuals report an overall lower quality of life, but the extent to which these issues are addressed during therapy evaluations has not been examined systematically.MethodologyIn this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we employ a rule-based NLP/lexicon-based approach to examine the areas of focus of therapy evaluations documented by occupational therapy, physical therapy (PT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) professionals. piezas.titulo: From virtual practice to real-world function the transfer problem in digital neurorehabilitation
piezas.resumenOriginal: Digital technologies have expanded opportunities for neurorehabilitation by enabling intensive, interactive, and adaptable motor practice. However, improvements achieved within virtual environments, rehabilitation games, or technology-based assessments do not necessarily translate into meaningful changes in everyday function. This Mini Review examines the transfer problem in digital neurorehabilitation and discusses key factors that may limit the generalization of training-related gains to real-world performance. We synthesize evidence regarding task specificity, sensory and perception-action differences between digital and physical environments, cognitive and contextual demands, practice variability, and patient-specific constraints that influence transfer. Based on these mechanisms, we propose a transfer-oriented framework consisting of five interconnected stages: skill acquisition, adaptive variability, cognitive-motor integration, contextualized real-world practice, and ecological evaluation. This framework emphasizes that transfer should be deliberately targeted rather than assumed as a consequence of successful digital training. We further discuss how virtual reality, augmented reality, wearable sensing, and hybrid rehabilitation models may support different stages of this process when integrated within adaptive and personalized approaches. Future digital rehabilitation research should move beyond evaluating performance within trained tasks and incorporate measures of functional and ecological transfer, including real-world mobility, activity, and participation. A shift from technology-centered rehabilitation toward transfer-oriented design may enhance the clinical impact of digital interventions and support meaningful improvements in daily life.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de practicar en pantalla: los avances en neurorehabilitación digital no garantizan mejoras en la vida cotidiana. This is the first of a two-part series exploring how Google Cloud is bringing the foundational values of a high-performance parallel filesystem–TB/s throughput, sub-ms latency at high client scale, and POSIX support–to a broader set of use cases and users. Historically, due to the cost and special purpose nature of parallel filesystems, colder data had to be stored outside of the filesystem and AI developers have had to maintain separate, slower environments for writing code, compiling libraries, and managing repositories. This fragmentation increases the toil of manual data staging, dataset copying, and managing disjointed namespaces. Google Cloud Managed Lustre is solving these problems through our 6 cents/GB*month Dynamic Tier and by optimizing Managed Lustre performance for a range of development tasks and workloads – making Managed Lustre a “One-Stop Shop” for high-performance AI and HPC workloads. Lower Cost: More Lustre for Less with the Dynamic Tier The Managed Lustre Dynamic Tier provides sub-ms latency for hot data, which allows you to store all of your data in a single namespace, and costs only 6 cents/GB*month . Throughput, capacity scale and client scale: Throughput scales linearly with capacity up to 80 PB, while sub-ms latency for hot data remains stable as you scale to tens of thousands of clients. Single-flat fee: Predictable pricing. No independent charges for disk media types, data movement within the namespace, or metadata IOPS. Write-Heavy Checkpointing: Bursty checkpoint writes land directly in the High Performance Cache. Older checkpoints are transparently demoted to the Capacity Pool (HDD). piezas.titulo: State-dependent responses of emotional brain networks in high myopia under blurred vision: a shift towards dorsal stream and cross-modal processing
piezas.resumenOriginal: PurposeReliable sensory input plays a vital role in shaping emotional experience, however, how the brain modulates the formation of emotion under chronic visual degradation remains unclear. Using high myopia (HM) as a natural model of sustained blur, this study investigated state-dependent responses of emotional brain networks during blurred movie viewing.MethodsTwenty-four participants with high myopia (HM) were tested without optical correction, comparing with normal vision (NV) controls from previous research. All participants watched thriller and scenic movie clips twice over one week during fMRI. Intra-subject synchrony and seed-based functional connectivity analyses focused on the amygdala and visual processing streams.ResultsCompared to NV controls, the HM group exhibited reduced intra-subject synchrony in visual cortices but increased synchrony in the primary auditory cortex, indicating cross-modal compensatory enhancement. During threat processing, HM participants showed strengthened and stable functional connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsal visual stream. For non-threatening content, this enhanced connectivity initially involved both dorsal and ventral stream but persisted selectively in the dorsal stream upon repeated viewing.ConclusionSustained visual blur elicits a perceptual-state-dependent functional response in emotional networks, characterized by heightened cross-modal auditory integration and an increased recruitment of the visual dorsal stream during blurred viewing. These findings highlight the brain’s immediate compensatory mechanisms under conditions of ambiguous visual input.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 4
piezas.resumenOriginal: In response to my last fragments (probably the bit about us worrying if LLMs have consciousness when we when we should be wondering why they don’t have a conscience) “Metalanguage” replied : we shipped the id and forgot the superego. classic software lifecycle. I don’t know what was on their mind, but their post immediately made me think of the classic 1956 movie Forbidden Planet. Plenty of sci-fi, and other literature, have explored humans creating technology with unintended behavior, going back at least to Mary Shelly. But that movie was particularly influential on sci-fi film-making and in the heart of its story is what happens when we nurture a thinking machine. I use the term “nurture” here deliberately. We talk of building software, but building implies a degree of determinism. When we build a bridge, or a locomotive, we expect it to behave in a controlled and well-understood manner. That’s a difference in degree to how we cultivate plants in our garden, or nurture young children. One of the challenges of working with these systems is understanding what has changed in this shift from building a computational system to nurturing an inferential one, and how our processes need to change in response. We get unintended behavior with deterministic building: some bridges have collapsed, and our computational systems often have bugs. But one difference is that when we find a bug in a computational system we can usually fix it. Even if we can’t, we can usually disable a component so the bug won’t do further harm. With inferential LLMs however, there is no such simple fix or disablement, which may lead us to the fate of the Krell. (If you haven’t seen Forbidden Planet, it’s well worth watching. Yes, it shows it was made in the 1950s - with special effects, music, acting, and attitudes of that decade. But the story is solid, and its key theme is very relevant to the future we build with generative AI. Just don’t read about it in advance, it’s better to be immersed in the story without spoilers - although my memory of that experience is understandably hazy.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Many people who follow me also know my friend Ola Bini, who was my colleague at Thoughtworks for many years, and was living in Ecuador working as an independent software security expert. Sadly his time in Ecuador was dogged by a bogus prosecution by the authorities there. But things seemed to have settled down, and although not allowed to leave Ecuador, Ola was able to get on with his life. Sadly that’s no longer the case as he was deported from Ecuador on Friday: According to information released by his lawyer, Bini was intercepted by a car with four people who identified themselves as immigration agents. He was then taken to an immigration office without further information or a formal order from a competent authority. There, officials told Bini that his visa had been revoked but didn’t show any supporting document. Bini’s defense filed a habeas corpus to safeguard his freedom and prevent his deportation. Yet, Ecuadorian authorities affirmed that the developer represents a threat or risk to public security and the state structure, and must leave the country. The ground for deportation is a secret report which allegedly asserts that Bini committed acts against the security of Ecuador. The defense could not access its contents. I was really worried for a while, since it wasn’t clear where he was going to be deported to. But he tweeted from Sweden , so I’m thankful for that. But this is only a partial relief. Ola has spent thirteen years in Ecuador and made it his home. To be thrown out of your home for scant reason is a heavy thing to bear, and the officials who did that have committed a serious offense. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ DDD Europe have released the video of Gien Verschatse interviewing Eric Evans and myself at the conference in June. We start by talking about how we bonded over conceptual modeling in the late 1990s. The conversation quickly moves to AI, we note that it’s impossible to predict how such a big change will work out. We do expect that it will cause us to think about our work in different ways, but the change may well be liberating, it’s reinvigorated Eric’s love of programming. people are probably going to feel very frustrated by [the new way of thinking about software]… but when you get through that, there is a kind of a wonderful feeling of my brain’s been loosened up. Our background in agile planning helps with the uncertainty, as we are used to taking small steps and being attentive to feedback. We mull on the interplay of writing and thinking, in terms of both prose and code, and how its very much an iterative process of exploration and refinement - the same is true when we chat with our LLMs. And don’t miss Eric’s important final tip. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Paul Graham: There were a lot of things that only worked because there’s a limit to the rate at which humans can operate. We’re about to find out what all of them are, as they break. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ The speculation continues about whether or not reading code will play a part in a software developer’s future. Geoffrey Huntley says . People are still saying, very loudly, that code should be readable so that humans can understand it. I no longer think that’s the goal. Interestingly his example has the LLM explain a haskell function definition… by translating it to Python. Which, to me, suggests there is a role for code - just that LLM need not store code in the same form that it presents it to a reader. This is essentially the same idea as projectional editing , which posits that the editable representation of software need not be the same as its storage representation. Sam Ruby touches on this as he muses on a Rails World keynote . He quotes DHH saying: Rust is a good prompt compilation target for the moment, but so is C++. And soon assembler. Then microcode. Myopic to think we’re going to stop the agentic drill bit until it reaches computing bedrock. He responds with: The post leaves one question unasked, though: what sits at the top of the drill? What do we keep, edit and trust as the source of truth? He carries out exercise of looking at some Rails software. Represented in Ruby/Rails and its about 60,000 tokens. Compiling it into C it turns into 4,000,000 tokens. That increase in token size will hamper the LLM, that still has to fit it into its context window, and even if it were to fit, figure out where to focus its attention. Sam points out reasons why, even absent a human reading it, it makes sense to represent the program in a higher-level language. what Rails becomes when agents write the code: the most compact, precise and conventional specification of a web application, whatever it ends up compiled to. Let the drill go as deep as it can. Just keep the notation at the top. This all reminds me of what Unmesh Joshi argued : that code serves “two distinct but intertwined purposes”: instructions to a machine, and a conceptual model of the problem domain. After exploring how those change with LLMs he concludes: The role of coding is not disappearing. But it is changing. As LLMs make code generation cheaper, the mechanical act of writing instructions becomes less central. What becomes more important is making the conceptual model explicit, discovering the right vocabulary, and refining that vocabulary through iteration, domain expertise, and feedback. This is also why programming languages continue to matter deeply. We are not meant to be passive reviewers of generated code. The act of writing code is itself part of our thinking. Code is still instructions for a machine. But it is also a model of understanding. In the LLM era, that second role becomes even more important. The future of coding is not just writing more code faster. It is building better conceptual models, better vocabularies, and better foundations on top of which both humans and LLMs can work. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ In a later post, Sam pondered on how people are talking about the capabilities of agents in a way that resembles the parable of the blind men and the elephant. We all only have only a partial view of this object and where it’s going. A theme for all of us: The practical question isn’t whether agents are good. It’s this: for the task in front of you this week, where will the information come from, and what will check the result? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ The Economist’s pithy summation of investors concerns about the dangers of AI companies’ products : It’s hard to celebrate an initial public offering that leads to a terminal public offing. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ The news about the latest model from Google is interesting . Gemini 4 Argon has an insanely low hallucination rate on Artificial Analysis. 15%. Grok 4.7 is at 29%. GPT-6 Astra 45%. Opus 5.5 59%. Fable 5.1 69%. The only models below it barely answer anything. None of them get more than 15% right. It gets fewer answers right than Opus 5.5 on max, 50% against 66%. But when it doesnt know, it says so instead of making something up. Being clearer about what it doesn’t know, at a cost of getting less answers right, is definitely a trade-off I prefer.

piezas.titulo: Somatosensory phenotyping in women with persistent genital arousal disorder: a case-control study.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Introduction Persistent genital arousal disorder (PGAD) is a rare and distressing condition characterized by persistent, unwanted genital arousal in the absence of sexual desire or stimulation. Persistent genital arousal disorder is increasingly recognized as a disorder of abnormal genital sensory processing, but objective neurophysiological data remain limited. Methods We conducted an exploratory case-control study to characterize somatosensory function in women with PGAD. Thirty women with PGAD and 30 age-matched healthy controls were recruited at Leiden University Medical Center. Participants underwent quantitative sensory testing (QST) at hand and external genital sites, conditioned pain modulation, and corneal confocal microscopy. Results Hand QST values were within normal range in both groups. In the genital region, PGAD participants showed altered thermal pain processing, with cold and heat hyperalgesia compared with controls. Mechanical pain thresholds did not differ between groups; however, PGAD participants reported higher pain intensity ratings to mechanical stimuli and showed significantly greater temporal summation of pain in genital regions. Genital dynamic mechanical allodynia occurred more frequently in PGAD participants but did not differ significantly at the group level. Conditioned pain modulation magnitude did not differ between groups and showed substantial interindividual variability. Corneal confocal microscopy abnormalities were observed in a proportion of participants in both groups without significant between-group differences. Discussion These findings show that QST is feasible in women with PGAD and indicate that PGAD is associated with altered somatosensory processing demonstrating genital thermal hypersensitivity and central pain sensitization in a subset of patients.

piezas.titulo: Digital phenotyping of migraine aura
piezas.resumenOriginal: Migraine aura is a transient, focal neurological phenomenon, characterized by evolving visual, somatosensory, language, and, to a lesser extent, motor disturbances, among other symptoms that reflect dynamic alterations in brain function, involving not only cortical, but also subcortical structures. Despite advances in understanding its neurobiology, including the role of cortical spreading depolarization, migraine aura remains incompletely characterized. This is most likely because of its unpredictable onset, brief duration, individual and symptom variability, and reliance on retrospective clinical assessment. Consequently, its temporal evolution and biological heterogeneity remain to be fully elucidated. Digital phenotyping has emerged as a framework for characterizing health and disease through continuous real-world data collected using personal digital technologies. Here we examine the rationale for considering the potential application of digital phenotyping to migraine aura. We argue that aura’s unique biological and temporal characteristics can make it a suitable choice for continuous multidimensional assessment. Integrating patient-reported symptoms with physiological, behavioral, and environmental data may improve phenotypic resolution. Consequently, it may help advance mechanistic understanding and capture within-person variability. Therefore, we present a conceptual framework alongside the methodological and translational challenges of digital phenotyping, including implementation-related challenges. Rather than replacing established clinical and neurobiological approaches, digital phenotyping is presented as a complementary framework that, if rigorously validated, could potentially advance our understanding of aura and migraine aura research, support the institution and consolidation of precision headache medicine, and facilitate patient care.
